Review unit 71–74: passive substitutes, function verbs, formal connectors.
It's 3 May 2034, 10:30 a.m., in front of the Pankow registry office. In half an hour Mara and Jakob are getting married. Ludwig is a witness. Lena, the second witness, is helping Mara with her dress.
Lena, I'm shaking. If only I were calmer!
You're the calmest bride I've ever seen. Jakob rang three times this morning because he couldn't tie his tie.
If only I'd taught him! So who tied it for him?
I did. At seven in the morning, in my kitchen. Just as I did for Jonas and for Thomas, thirty years ago. It's my speciality.
Ludwig, if only Friedrich were here. And Grandma Ingrid. I never knew her, but I have the feeling that today she's part of all this.
They are here. Friedrich is sitting in the front row, in the seat Grete has kept free for him. And Ingrid is outside, on a street sign. You'll walk past her today.
Grandpa, have you got the speech for the party?
I've got a toast. Three sentences. The first begins with “Möge”. It sounds old-fashioned, but at a wedding it fits.
“Möge”? Like in fairy tales? “May your life be long and happy”?
Almost. You'll hear. And now come on. Mrs Kranz doesn't wait. She has thirty years of experience and zero patience.
Wait! The bridal bouquet! Where's the bridal bouquet?
White lilac. From Grete. She gave it to me this morning. She said it brought luck once before.
What we would like now, but isn't the case. Konjunktiv II + “doch” / “nur” / “bloß”. Two versions:
Wenn es doch nicht regnen würde!
“doch”, “nur” and “bloß” are obligatory here: without them the sentence sounds unfinished (like a condition without a consequence).
If only I had come too!
If only we had asked him once!
Apart from reported speech, Konjunktiv I also appears in fixed formulas of good wishes and in solemn texts:
In today's German, “Möge…” sounds festive and a little old-fashioned — perfect for weddings, christenings and speeches. In everyday life you say: “Ich wünsche euch, dass…”
Darf ich kurz um eure Aufmerksamkeit bitten?
Ich kenne die Braut seit … / Als ich Jakob zum ersten Mal sah, …
Ich erinnere mich noch genau an den Tag, als …
Lasst uns die Gläser erheben! Auf das Brautpaar!
A good toast is short: 1–2 minutes. The Germans have a saying: “Eine gute Rede hat einen guten Anfang und ein gutes Ende — und beide möglichst dicht beieinander.”
Let's raise a glass to the bride and groom!
If only I had known that!
If only I had more time!

The third of May 2034 was a Wednesday and it wasn't raining. Mara hadn't asked for that, but Elif had apparently ordered it anyway, because when the small group stood in front of the Pankow registry office at half past ten, a mild spring sun was shining on the old brick building, and blackbirds were singing in the lime trees in front of the entrance. It was a small group, as Mara and Jakob had wished: forty people, most of them from a single building on Kastanienallee, a few from Thuringia, two from Sibiu.

Dan and Elena had come on Sunday, by plane, with two suitcases, one of which contained nothing but honey, țuică (plum brandy) and a tablecloth that Elena had kept for thirty years for her daughter's wedding. Jakob's mother, Mrs Lorenz, a small, energetic woman from a village near Weimar, had come by train, with a basket full of Thuringian sausages, because she didn't trust Berlin meat. The two mothers had met on Monday at the café “Bei Ingrid” for the first time, without a common language, and after ten minutes they had started showing each other photos of their children as babies. After an hour they were, as Lena put it, “a dangerous team”.

On Tuesday evening, the evening before the wedding, there had been a “Polterabend” in the courtyard on Kastanienallee, at the wish of Mrs Lorenz, who had insisted that a Thuringian can't get married without a “Polterabend”. The neighbours had brought old china, cracked plates, cups without handles, and thrown them onto the paving, roaring with laughter. Elif had sacrificed an ugly vase from the family's cellar, Mr Yilmaz a whole stack of saucers. And then Mara and Jakob had swept up the shards together for a whole hour, in the lamplight, while Ludwig watched from the window and said: “That's marriage. Others make the mess, and you clear it up together.”

At eleven, Mrs Kranz opened the door of the wedding room. It was a bright, simple room with tall windows, two rows of chairs and a table with a white tablecloth and a bunch of tulips. Mrs Kranz was wearing a navy suit and the same rimless glasses as always, but Mara noticed at once that on the wall behind her, next to her granddaughter's drawing, the little jar of honey from Sibiu was still there. Mrs Kranz looked at her and, for the second time since Mara had known her, smiled.

In the front row sat the parents, Dan and Elena, Mrs Lorenz, and Andrei, who quietly translated everything for his parents the whole time. Beside them, in a wheelchair, because the way from the care home would have been too long, sat Grete, in black, with her pearl necklace. Next to her was an empty chair. Nobody sat on it. On the chair lay a single sprig of white lilac. Kuba sat in the second row, with a little velvet cushion on his knees, on which lay the two wedding rings. He was fourteen and wearing a suit for the first time, and five years ago, at the age of ten, he had announced that he would be a witness at this wedding. He wasn't allowed to be a witness, he was too young. But ring bearer, yes.

The ceremony lasted eighteen minutes. Mrs Kranz spoke briefly and clearly, without big words, as was her way. She said that in thirty years she had married more than five thousand couples and had learned that a good marriage isn't recognised by the size of the party, but by who comes to the party. “And when I look at this room,” she said, “I have no worries at all about this marriage.” Then she asked Jakob whether he wanted to marry Mara, and Jakob said “Yes” so loudly that Dan jumped in the front row. Then she asked Mara. Mara looked at Jakob, at the white lilac in her hands, at the empty chair next to Grete, and said: “Yes.” Quietly, but everyone heard.

Then they put on the rings. Kuba stood up with the velvet cushion and took the three steps forward as solemnly as if he were carrying the crown jewels. His hands were trembling. Jakob's ring was a simple gold band, which Jakob had ordered from a small workshop in Prenzlauer Berg, made from the gold of an old brooch of his grandmother Hilde's. Mara's ring was Hilde's own ring, thin and golden, with the little blue stone, which Jakob had given her in June in Kollwitzpark. When Mara let him put it on her finger, for the second time, this time for ever, she saw that Jakob's mother was crying in the front row. Hilde had been her mother.

Then the two of them signed. Then the witnesses signed: first Lena, her hands trembling, then Ludwig, slowly, carefully, with the old fountain pen Ingrid had given him on their twentieth wedding anniversary. His signature was large and a little crooked, and Mrs Kranz looked at it for a long time before putting the stamp underneath. “Mr Brandt,” she said quietly, so that only he could hear, “you have very beautiful handwriting. As if from another era.” Ludwig nodded. “My wife taught me,” he said. “My writing was very ugly when we met. She said she wouldn't marry a man whose love letters she couldn't read.”

The party was at the café “Bei Ingrid”, of course. Lena had pushed the tables together into one long table, with Elena's thirty-year-old tablecloth on it, and in the middle stood Andrei's wedding cake, three tiers, as he had threatened, with honey from Dan's hives and a little marzipan tram on the very top, with the number 46. There were sarmale (stuffed cabbage rolls) from Elena, Thuringian sausages from Mrs Lorenz, and Ayşe Yilmaz brought, without anyone asking her, two huge trays of börek. The brass bell by the door rang all afternoon, because every child who came in had to try it.

At four o'clock, Ludwig stood up. He tapped his glass with a spoon and the café went quiet, except for Fritz, who was snoring under the table. Ludwig had no sheet of paper. He had said he didn't need one for three sentences. He looked at Mara, who was sitting next to Jakob in her simple white dress, with Hilde's ring on her finger and Grete's lilac in a vase in front of her. He looked at Jakob, whose tie was still tied exactly the way Ludwig had tied it that morning. And he gave his toast.
Before that, Andrei had cut the cake together with the bride and groom, carefully taken the marzipan tram off the top and given it to Ludwig, who put it in his jacket pocket, next to the brass bell.

Seven years ago, a young woman with a suitcase stood in the stairwell at Kastanienallee thirty-one and asked me where the third floor was. I showed her the way. Since then she has shown each of us one. May your house always sing too, as ours has sung since you've been here. And never forget that sometimes you have to wait a long time for the most important thing, but that it comes. Long live the bride and groom!

It was more than three sentences. And nobody counted. Forty glasses were raised, Dan shouted “Să trăiască!” (“Long may they live!”), and Mrs Lorenz shouted “Hoch sollen sie leben!”, and then everyone sang all at once, in Romanian and in German, and Kuba pressed the brass bell so many times that Lena finally had to take it away from him. Grete, in her wheelchair by the window, raised her glass a little higher than the others, towards the chair next to her, which had been left empty here too. Mara saw. She stood up, went over to Grete, knelt beside the wheelchair in her white dress, and clinked glasses with her. “To Friedrich,” she said quietly. “To Friedrich,” said Grete. “If only he had been here. He would have loved to dance. He couldn't dance, but he would have loved to.”

And then Jakob danced with Mara, to a waltz that Mirko played on the viola, in the middle of the tables in the café, and Dan danced with Mrs Lorenz, Andrei with Lena, and Elif with Ludwig, slowly, very slowly, with his stick in one hand. Outside, in Ingrid-Brandt-Platz, a tram stopped at the stop, and the driver, who wasn't a driver but an apprentice with an old badge on his jacket, rang the bell twice. You could hear it through the café window. And Ludwig, in the middle of the dance, smiled and said to Elif: “Hear that? That's Leo. He's congratulating them.”

Late in the evening, when the last guests had left and Lena was putting the chairs up on the tables, Mara and Jakob sat with Grete by the window for a while. They told her about their honeymoon. They weren't going to Italy or to the Mediterranean. On Saturday they were going to Travemünde, with Grete and Sophie, by train, and on Sunday morning, where the Trave flows into the Baltic Sea, in front of the old house An der Trave, they were going to scatter Friedrich's ashes in the sea, as he had wished. And afterwards Mara and Jakob were going to stay on for a week, just the two of them, in a small guest house on the beach. Grete listened to them with her eyes closed and said nothing for a long time. Then at last she said: “Children, that's the craziest honeymoon I've ever heard of.” And then, more quietly: “Thank you.”

Read about wedding customs in Germany. Listen twice. At the end there are 4 questions.
In Germany only the civil wedding is legally valid. Anyone who wants a church wedding usually has one in addition.
On the evening before the wedding many couples celebrate a “Polterabend”: friends smash china, because the shards are said to bring luck.
The bride and groom then have to clear up the shards together. May they solve all their problems together later on too!
Another custom is log sawing: the couple saw through a wooden log together.
And at the end of the party people often shout: “Long live the bride and groom!”
the eve of the wedding (with smashing of crockery)
